stories.headline: COP31 talks collapse in Antalya over fossil-fuel transition
stories.summary: The COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended without an agreed pact after negotiators could not reaffirm a transition away from fossil fuels. The deadlock came days after the leaders of China, Russia and the United States declared plans to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. Frustration over fossil fuels dominated the talks, with observers warning that countries may pursue phase-out efforts outside the official UN process. India pressed the question of how fast emissions should fall, who will finance the transition, and how soon protection will reach vulnerable populations. Developed nations were urged to bear a greater share of the cost of historical carbon emissions.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests the viability of consensus-based UN climate diplomacy and the CBDR-RC principle; directly relevant to GS-III environment and GS-II global governance.

perspectives.take: Frames the collapse as a turning point that may push countries to pursue fossil-fuel phase-out outside official UN talks.

static.topic: Climate Change Regime & India's Commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle. Paris uses NDCs and a ratchet mechanism. Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and LiFE mission.
static.socioEconomic: Developing countries face gaps in climate finance and technology transfer; CBDR-RC underpins their demand for equitable burden-sharing.
static.whyInNews: COP31 in Antalya collapsed without a pact reaffirming a transition away from fossil fuels, raising questions about the UNFCCC process and equity.
static.wayForward: Bridge climate finance and technology gaps, operationalise the Loss & Damage fund, and pursue a just transition consistent with CBDR-RC.
prelimsPointers: India's updated NDC: cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 by 2030.
Paris Agreement goal: keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.
static.mainsAngle: Climate finance and technology transfer gaps; examine equity in the Global Stocktake and just transition.

static.topic: United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.socioEconomic: Representation and veto politics shape multilateral outcomes; developing countries seek greater voice in global governance.
static.whyInNews: The COP31 deadlock highlights the limits of consensus-based UN multilateralism and renews debate on institutional reform.
static.wayForward: Advance IGN discussions, address veto politics, and make multilateral bodies more representative and effective.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN HQ is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim rests on representativeness, its population and contributions; assess obstacles (veto politics, Africa's Ezulwini Consensus).

static.topic: India's Foreign Policy & Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks. It engages across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA simultaneously.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and Quad (with US, Japan, Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.socioEconomic: India balances development needs with climate action and speaks for the Global South in climate finance and equity debates.
static.whyInNews: At COP31, India asked how fast emissions should fall, who will finance the transition, and how soon protection will reach people already facing climate impacts.
static.wayForward: Continue strategic autonomy and coalition-building with the Global South to shape equitable climate and development outcomes.

stories.headline: Modi unveils ₹15,000-crore Nepal package, IIT campus as Balen Shah visits Delhi
stories.summary: During Nepali Prime Minister Balen Shah's first visit to India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a development package of over ₹15,000 crore (roughly $1.6 billion) for Nepal. Eight agreements were signed spanning trade, infrastructure, energy and technology, and the two sides flagged new port access, rail links, hydropower cooperation and an offshore IIT campus in Nepal. Alongside the campus, India announced a startup incubator, an innovation hub and scholarships for Nepali students in India. A large part of the assistance is being framed as support for reconstruction in a Nepal recently hit by severe floods, while Indian commentary reads the package as an effort to deepen ties amid China's expanding footprint in Kathmandu.
stories.whyItMatters: India–Nepal ties sit at the core of the Neighbourhood First policy and are a recurring GS-II question on development assistance, connectivity diplomacy and India–China competition in South Asia. The education and infrastructure components also feed GS-II governance and GS-III infrastructure/investment themes.

static.topic: India–Nepal Relations: The 1950 Treaty and the Open Border
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood (South Asia)
static.whatIsIt: The India–Nepal relationship rests on the Treaty of Peace and Friendship (1950), which underpins an open border permitting free movement of people, and on a dense web of trade, transit, water-sharing and security arrangements. It is the template on which India's Nepal policy — aid, connectivity and defence consultations — is built.
static.background: The Treaty of Peace and Friendship was signed in 1950, followed by a Trade and Transit Treaty in 1954, revised in 1996. The Mahakali Treaty (1996) covers the Sarada Barrage, Tanakpur Barrage and the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project. Nepal's 2015 Constitution triggered Madhesi protests and a prolonged disruption of supplies across the border. The Eminent Persons' Group (EPG) set up by both governments submitted its report on revising the treaty framework in 2018; it has not been implemented. Nepal joined China's Belt and Road Initiative in 2017, and ratified the US MCC compact in 2022. Cartographic disputes over Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura have periodically strained ties.
static.geography: Nepal is landlocked, bordered by India to the south, east and west and by China (Tibet) to the north. The open India–Nepal border runs through five Indian States — Sikkim, West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Kalapani lies at the India–Nepal–China trijunction. Nepal's rivers (Kosi, Gandak, Karnali) drain into the Ganga basin.
static.socioEconomic: Nepal's economy is closely tied to India through trade, transit routes, remittances and labour movement; India is Nepal's largest trading partner. Hydropower is Nepal's principal export-oriented resource, and Indian public sector firms are involved in projects such as Arun-III. Gorkha recruitment into the Indian Army remains a sensitive legacy issue.
static.whyInNews: Prime Minister Balen Shah's first visit to India produced a package of over ₹15,000 crore, eight signed pacts, new port access and rail links, and plans for an offshore IIT campus — the latest chapter in a relationship governed by the 1950 treaty framework.
static.wayForward: Progress on the Pancheshwar project, early conclusion of a revised transit/trade framework, and resolution of boundary questions through the existing bilateral mechanisms would help convert announcements into durable outcomes. Managing asymmetry through sensitivity to Nepali sovereignty concerns is central.
prelimsPointers: Nepal is landlocked: India borders it on the south, east and west; China (Tibet) lies to the north.
The Mahakali Treaty (1996) covers the Sarada Barrage, Tanakpur Barrage and the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project.
Nepal's Kosi, Gandak and Karnali rivers are part of the Ganga basin; the Kosi is known as the 'Sorrow of Bihar'.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the 1950 treaty framework and the open border shape India's leverage and Nepal's sensitivities. Discuss whether asymmetry in the relationship is best managed through aid and connectivity or through institutional revision of the treaty.

static.topic: Neighbourhood First and India's Development Assistance Diplomacy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India's Neighbourhood Policy and Development Cooperation
static.whatIsIt: India's Neighbourhood First policy prioritises grant assistance, concessional credit, connectivity and capacity-building in South Asia. In Nepal, this has taken the form of Line of Credit-funded infrastructure, petroleum pipelines, rail links, hydropower cooperation and, most recently, education institutions.
static.background: The Gujral Doctrine (1996) framed the principle of non-reciprocal concessions to smaller neighbours. Neighbourhood First became an explicit policy thrust from 2014, supported by EXIM Bank Lines of Credit and grant projects. The Motihari–Amlekhgunj petroleum products pipeline, operational in 2019, was India's first cross-border petroleum products pipeline in South Asia. The BBIN framework and proposals such as the Raxaul–Kathmandu rail link illustrate the connectivity approach. Nepal's BRI membership and Chinese infrastructure engagement have added a competitive dimension.
static.geography: India's connectivity projects with Nepal run through the Bihar and Uttar Pradesh border corridors, linking Kathmandu to Kolkata/Haldia and Visakhapatnam port access routes.
static.socioEconomic: Development assistance builds goodwill, expands Indian market access and creates interdependencies. Critically, large credit lines raise debt-sustainability questions in a small economy and can provoke sovereignty sensitivities.
static.whyInNews: The ₹15,000-crore-plus package, eight pacts, new port access, rail links and an offshore IIT campus are a fresh test of whether Indian assistance can translate into durable influence in Nepal.
static.wayForward: Shift the emphasis from headline announcements to delivery timelines, local capacity-building and transparent financing terms, while coordinating with Nepal's own development priorities rather than framing projects competitively.
prelimsPointers: The Motihari–Amlekhgunj pipeline, operational in 2019, was India's first cross-border petroleum products pipeline in South Asia.
BBIN stands for Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal — the sub-regional cooperation framework.
Lines of Credit for such projects are extended through the EXIM Bank of India.
static.mainsAngle: Critically evaluate India's development assistance as an instrument of influence in South Asia. Does connectivity-and-aid diplomacy deliver durable goodwill, or does it invite charges of asymmetry and debt dependence?

static.topic: Himalayan Rivers, Monsoon Floods and Disaster Management
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography of India (Himalayan rivers and the monsoon); links to disaster management
static.whatIsIt: The Himalayan river system is snow-fed and perennial, and Nepal's Kosi, Gandak and Karnali rivers carry monsoon discharge into the Ganga basin. Because the monsoon delivers roughly three-fourths of annual rainfall in June–September, the Nepal–Bihar plains corridor is acutely flood-prone.
static.background: The Indian monsoon is driven by differential heating, the northward shift of the ITCZ and the Tibetan Plateau's role as a heat pump. El Niño typically weakens the monsoon, La Niña strengthens it, and the Indian Ocean Dipole modulates it. Historical flood disasters in the Kosi basin and the 2015 Nepal earthquake illustrate the trans-boundary nature of Himalayan hazard risk. Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) are an emerging high-altitude threat.
static.geography: Nepal's rivers descend steeply from the Himalaya onto the Gangetic plains, carrying heavy sediment loads that shift channels and breach embankments. Shared river basins mean flood risk in Nepal translates directly into flooding in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
static.socioEconomic: Recurrent flooding damages agriculture, roads and hydropower assets, displacing communities and imposing repeated reconstruction costs on both countries — the context in which flood-reconstruction assistance is announced.
static.whyInNews: A significant share of India's ₹15,000-crore package is presented by several outlets as reconstruction support for flood-affected Nepal, tying the announcement to trans-boundary disaster risk.
static.wayForward: Strengthen joint flood forecasting and early warning, share hydrological data in real time, invest in GLOF risk mapping, and integrate embankment and catchment management across the Nepal–India border.
prelimsPointers: Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed), whereas peninsular rivers are largely seasonal and rain-fed.
The monsoon delivers roughly 75% of India's annual rainfall during June–September.
Nepal's Kosi, Gandak and Karnali rivers drain into the Ganga basin.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how trans-boundary river basins and monsoon variability make disaster risk a shared India–Nepal challenge, and assess the role of joint forecasting, data-sharing and basin-level management in reducing flood losses.

prelims: India announced a development package of over ₹15,000 crore — reported as roughly $1.6 billion / $1.62 billion — for Nepal during PM Balen Shah's visit to Delhi.
Eight agreements were signed covering trade, infrastructure, energy and technology, alongside plans for new port access, rail links and hydropower projects.
India will set up an offshore IIT campus in Nepal, plus a startup incubator, an innovation hub, and scholarships for Nepali students in India.
A portion of the assistance is framed as reconstruction support for Nepal following severe floods.
stories.mainsQuestion: India's ₹15,000-crore package for Nepal combines reconstruction aid, connectivity and education diplomacy. Critically examine whether such assistance can secure durable Indian influence in Nepal, given Nepal's sensitivity to asymmetry and China's expanding footprint in the region.

stories.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after US government push; AI stocks surge
stories.summary: Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia's President, CEO and board director, days after resigning, following a board decision the company said came after a series of meetings and input from 'senior levels of the United States government'. US President Donald Trump welcomed the move as 'correct and proper' and claimed 'I made the deal', while officials indicated there was no risk to national security. The crisis was triggered by US scrutiny of Alice Huang — reported to be at the centre of an affair — over alleged contacts with a Chinese spy agency, and by fears in Washington that Huang's exit would weaken American competitiveness in artificial intelligence. Markets reacted sharply: Nvidia shares rose about 31%, adding roughly $1 trillion to the company's value, and Reuters estimated the AI rally would add about $2 trillion to the Nasdaq-100, reversing the previous week's global selloff.
stories.whyItMatters: A live case study for GS-III on state–market relations in strategic technologies and for GS-II on technology as an instrument of national power; it also illustrates concentration risk in global equity markets and its spillovers to India.

perspectives.take: Straight institutional reporting: the board acted after input from senior US government levels, and Trump called it a 'correct and proper decision'.

Explains the political economy — Trump intervened fearing Huang's exit would weaken US AI competitiveness and deepen market turmoil; also carries the 31% share surge and the national-security reassurance.

static.topic: India Semiconductor Mission and chip-making policy
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Industry, Infrastructure and Investment; Semiconductor Ecosystem
static.whatIsIt: The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) is the nodal agency under MeitY, set up under the Semicon India Programme, to build a domestic fabrication, packaging, design and compound-semiconductor ecosystem through fiscal support to approved projects.
static.background: Announced in December 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore, the Semicon India Programme offers fiscal support of up to 50% of project cost for approved fab and packaging units, and works alongside the Design Linked Incentive scheme and state policies. Earlier attempts include the 2007 semiconductor policy and electronics manufacturing cluster schemes; the current push has drawn proposals from global and domestic players, though most approved projects are at packaging, testing or design stage rather than leading-edge fabrication.
static.geography: Approved and proposed projects cluster in Gujarat (Sanand, Dholera), Assam (Morigaon) and Uttar Pradesh (Jewar), drawing on industrial corridors, port access and existing electronics clusters.
static.socioEconomic: Fabs are capital-, water- and skill-intensive; the ecosystem creates high-wage design and engineering jobs but limited mass employment, so welfare gains depend on ancillary electronics manufacturing and skilling.
static.whyInNews: The Nvidia episode — where one chipmaker's leadership change moved global markets by trillions — shows why states treat chip supply chains as strategic, reinforcing the rationale for India's own fabrication push.
static.wayForward: Maintain policy stability and fiscal support across electoral cycles, prioritise compound semiconductors and ATMP/packaging where entry barriers are lower, tie incentives to skilling and R&D, and secure water and critical-mineral inputs.
prelimsPointers: The India Semiconductor Mission functions under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).
Fiscal support under the Semicon India Programme is up to 50% of project cost for approved fab and packaging projects.
India imports the bulk of its semiconductor requirement; the ISM aims to reduce this dependence.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's semiconductor incentives should prioritise leading-edge fabrication or downstream packaging and design, given capital, water and skill constraints.

static.topic: Artificial Intelligence governance and regulation
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — IT, AI and Effects of Technology on Society; Governance
static.whatIsIt: AI governance refers to the laws, standards and institutions — from data protection and algorithmic accountability to compute access and model safety — that steer the development and deployment of artificial intelligence.
static.background: The EU's AI Act (2024) introduced a risk-based regulatory framework; the US has relied more on executive orders and voluntary commitments; India's IndiaAI Mission (approved 2024, outlay about ₹10,372 crore) focuses on compute, datasets, application development, skilling and safe AI. Multilateral efforts include the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) and a UN advisory body on AI governance, while the 2023 Bletchley Park and 2024 Seoul summits shaped the frontier-AI safety agenda.
static.socioEconomic: AI concentrates market power in a few firms with compute and data advantages; debates centre on job displacement, bias, misinformation and the divide between compute-rich and compute-poor countries.
static.whyInNews: The reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after government intervention shows AI capability is now treated as a strategic national asset, sharpening the case for regulation balancing innovation, safety and sovereignty.
static.wayForward: Adopt a risk-tiered, technology-neutral framework; invest in public compute and datasets; mandate transparency for high-risk uses; and build institutional capacity for audit and redress.
prelimsPointers: The EU AI Act (2024) is the first comprehensive, risk-tiered AI law.
The IndiaAI Mission was approved in 2024 with an outlay of about ₹10,372 crore.
GPAI is a multi-stakeholder initiative on responsible AI; India is a member.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the elements of a regulatory framework for AI that reconciles innovation, national security and fundamental rights in India.

static.topic: US–China technology rivalry and export controls
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of Policies and Politics of Developed and Developing Countries on India's Interests
static.whatIsIt: Export controls are unilateral restrictions on the sale of sensitive technologies — advanced semiconductors, chip-making equipment and AI accelerators — used by the US to slow China's access to frontier computing.
static.background: The US tightened controls on advanced chip and equipment exports to China from October 2022 and broadened them in 2023, while the CHIPS and Science Act (2022) committed about $52.7 billion to domestic semiconductor manufacturing and R&D. China has responded with export curbs on gallium, germanium and graphite and a push for self-reliance. India is not a direct party but is exposed through supply chains, price effects and its own strategic choices.
static.socioEconomic: Controls raise costs and fragment supply chains, pushing 'friend-shoring' and duplicate capacity; for India they create both investment opportunities and risks of technology lock-out.
static.whyInNews: Washington's direct involvement in Nvidia's leadership decision is read as an extension of the same logic — treating AI chip leadership as a national-security asset.
static.wayForward: India should deepen trusted-supply-chain partnerships, negotiate technology-transfer and critical-minerals arrangements, and build domestic design capability rather than relying on either bloc.
prelimsPointers: The CHIPS and Science Act (2022) committed about $52.7 billion to US semiconductor manufacturing and R&D.
The US Entity List restricts exports to named foreign firms on national-security grounds.
China has imposed export controls on gallium and germanium, key inputs for chips and optics.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how US–China technology decoupling affects India's semiconductor ambitions and strategic autonomy.

stories.headline: Supreme Court orders more SIR tribunals, priority for deleted voters' appeals in Bengal
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has directed the Election Commission of India to expand the number of appellate tribunals handling appeals arising from the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal. The Court asked that appeals filed by electors whose names have been deleted be taken up on priority, while appeals challenging inclusions be deferred for the time being. The direction is intended to clear a backlog of statutory appeals under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, which currently lie before designated appellate authorities, usually the District Magistrate or an Additional District Magistrate. The order keeps the SIR process itself undisturbed but strengthens the remedial channel available to aggrieved voters before the rolls are finalised.
stories.whyItMatters: Electoral roll revision and the appellate remedy against wrongful deletion sit at the intersection of Article 324, the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the right to vote — a recurring GS-II theme on the integrity of electoral machinery and judicial oversight of the ECI.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court issued directions to the Election Commission on the handling of SIR-related appeals in West Bengal, exercising its supervisory jurisdiction over a constitutional authority.
static.wayForward: Continued monitoring of compliance with procedural safeguards, while balancing judicial oversight of the ECI against the Commission's constitutionally guaranteed functional autonomy under Article 324.

static.topic: Electoral Roll Revision and Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Constitutional Bodies (Election Commission) and Elections
static.whatIsIt: Preparation and revision of electoral rolls is done by the Election Commission of India under Article 324 read with the Representation of the People Act, 1950. SIR is a door-to-door, intensive verification exercise in which existing rolls are re-verified and entries of dead, shifted or duplicate electors are removed, followed by fresh claims and objections.
static.background: The ECI conducts annual summary revision (SSR) and, less frequently, intensive revision. SIR has been carried out in the past, including in Andhra Pradesh (2002) and more recently in Bihar (2025). Under Section 22 of the RP Act, 1950, a person aggrieved by an order of the Electoral Registration Officer may appeal within 15 days to an appellate authority designated by the ECI, ordinarily the District Magistrate or Additional District Magistrate; appeals against orders of the District Election Officer lie to the Chief Electoral Officer under Section 23.
static.geography: West Bengal — 42 Lok Sabha and 294 assembly constituencies; the state is the site of the current SIR-related litigation.
static.socioEconomic: Deletion of genuine electors disproportionately affects the poor, migrants, women and the elderly, who often lack documentary proof of residence; an accessible appellate remedy is therefore central to electoral inclusion.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court directed the ECI to increase the number of appellate tribunals in West Bengal and to prioritise appeals filed by deleted voters, deferring appeals against inclusions.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the appellate mechanism with adequate tribunals, transparent reasons for deletion, wider publicity of appeal rights and timelines, and use of digital verification tools so that no bona fide elector is disenfranchised.
keyTerms: Appellate authority under Section 22, RP Act 1950
prelimsPointers: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission of India.
Article 326 provides for adult suffrage; Article 325 bars exclusion from rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
Appeal against an ERO order lies within 15 days to the appellate authority designated by the ECI under Section 22, RP Act 1950.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether intensive roll-revision exercises are compatible with the constitutional guarantee of universal adult suffrage, and evaluate the adequacy of statutory appellate remedies against wrongful deletion.

stories.headline: Rohingya welcome ICJ genocide verdict, but return to Myanmar remains distant
stories.summary: Rohingya refugees living in camps in Bangladesh have welcomed the International Court of Justice's verdict in the genocide case concerning Myanmar, treating it as international recognition of the atrocities they suffered. At the same time, refugee voices reported from the camps stress that legal vindication is not the same as a durable solution — most say they want to go back to Myanmar, but only when it is safe and their citizenship and rights are restored. Indian commentary frames the ruling as a moral and legal milestone while cautioning that enforcement depends on political will, since the ICJ has no independent police power and compliance rests on state consent and Security Council action. Editorials argue that the verdict's real test lies in whether Myanmar's political trajectory — currently dominated by military rule and ongoing conflict — can move towards democratic, accountable governance that would make return possible. The consolidated picture: a significant legal advance for accountability, but a humanitarian and political impasse that persists for the roughly million-strong displaced Rohingya population.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests how international judicial bodies deliver accountability when enforcement depends on political will — a recurring UPSC theme on the UN system, international law and refugee protection. Also links to India's neighbourhood policy, its non-signatory status to the Refugee Convention, and the Rohingya deportation litigation in Indian courts.

perspectives.take: Ground-level, refugee-centred framing: camp residents in Bangladesh celebrate the verdict as validation of their suffering but emphasise that their priority is safe, dignified return to Myanmar — not permanent displacement.
Analytical editorial line: the verdict is just, but Rohingya return is contingent on Myanmar turning democratic; legal outcomes alone cannot substitute for political change and accountability.
Cautiously hopeful editorial framing — 'some hope' — acknowledging the verdict as progress on the long road to justice while underlining the gap between judicial pronouncement and actual redress.

static.topic: United Nations & Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance / UN and its organs
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. The International Court of Justice, seated at The Hague, is the principal judicial organ and settles disputes between states and gives advisory opinions.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for UNSC expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive. The ICJ's effectiveness has historically been constrained by the absence of an independent enforcement mechanism — compliance depends on state consent and, in some cases, referral to the Security Council.
static.geography: ICJ sits at the Peace Palace, The Hague, Netherlands; UN headquarters in New York.
static.socioEconomic: Enforcement gaps in international justice disproportionately affect displaced and stateless populations, who lack a state to champion their claims.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ's verdict in the genocide case concerning Myanmar has been welcomed by Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, reviving debate on the enforceability of international judicial rulings.
static.wayForward: Strengthen compliance mechanisms, expand UNSC reform to improve representativeness, and build regional and multilateral pressure so that judicial findings translate into accountability and durable solutions for affected populations.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN HQ is in New York.

static.topic: Genocide Convention, 1948 and ICJ Jurisdiction
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law and Institutions
static.whatIsIt: The Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (1948) codifies genocide as an international crime and obliges states to prevent and punish it. Article IX of the Convention allows disputes between parties, including over state responsibility, to be taken to the ICJ.
static.background: The Convention was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948 in the aftermath of the Holocaust and entered into force in 1951. In 2019, The Gambia filed a case against Myanmar at the ICJ alleging violations of the Genocide Convention in relation to the Rohingya; the Court ordered provisional measures in January 2020 directing Myanmar to prevent genocidal acts and preserve evidence. The case has since proceeded through jurisdictional and merits stages.
static.geography: Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim minority concentrated in Myanmar's Rakhine State; large refugee populations live in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh.
static.socioEconomic: Statelessness, denial of citizenship under Myanmar's 1982 citizenship law, and camp-based dependency have left the Rohingya among the world's most protracted displaced populations.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ's verdict in the case has been welcomed by Rohingya refugees, who nonetheless stress that return to Myanmar remains their goal.
static.wayForward: Full compliance with provisional measures, preservation of evidence, cooperation with accountability mechanisms, and a political settlement in Myanmar that restores citizenship and rights are prerequisites for safe return.
prelimsPointers: The Genocide Convention was adopted in 1948 and entered into force in 1951.
The ICJ case against Myanmar was filed by The Gambia in 2019; provisional measures were ordered in January 2020.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the significance and limitations of the Genocide Convention in delivering justice to displaced communities, with reference to the Rohingya case.

static.topic: India and Refugee Protection Framework
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; Governance — refugee policy
static.whatIsIt: India has no dedicated domestic refugee law and is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol. Refugees are dealt with under the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 and executive discretion, with UNHCR playing a limited role.
static.background: India has historically hosted large refugee populations — Tibetans from 1959, Sri Lankans, Chakmas and Hajongs, and Rohingya who began arriving in significant numbers after 2012 and especially after 2017. In 2021, the Supreme Court in Mohammad Salimullah v. Union of India declined to restrain the government from deporting Rohingya refugees who had been detained, while noting the matter involved competing considerations of national security and humanitarian obligations.
static.geography: Rohingya refugees in India are dispersed across states including Jammu, Hyderabad, Delhi and parts of the North-East; the largest concentrations remain in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar.
static.socioEconomic: Refugee inflows raise questions of shelter, livelihood, documentation, access to education and health, and pressure on local infrastructure in host regions.
static.whyInNews: Renewed international attention on Rohingya displacement following the ICJ verdict has revived debate on India's refugee policy and its treatment of Rohingya within its borders.
static.wayForward: Consider a domestic refugee law framework with clear status-determination procedures, balanced against security concerns; continue humanitarian assistance and support regional burden-sharing with Bangladesh.

prelimsPointers: India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol.
India has no standalone domestic refugee legislation; entry and stay are governed by the Foreigners Act, 1946 and the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920.

stories.headline: Ukraine strikes Russian warship in Libya, widening war's reach
stories.summary: Ukraine carried out a long-range strike on a Russian warship at a port in Libya, according to reports, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailing the operation. The target was said to be about 2,400 kilometres from the front line in Ukraine, making it one of Kyiv's most distant attacks of the war. BBC analysis described the sinking as an escalation that illustrates how the conflict is spreading beyond the immediate battlefield. The episode has drawn attention to Libya's role as a fragile, externally contested space and to the risks of war expanding into third countries.
stories.whyItMatters: For UPSC, it links the Russia-Ukraine war to maritime security, international law, and the geopolitics of Libya and the Mediterranean. It also tests the limits of sovereignty when belligerents operate in third states.

perspectives.take: Frames the strike as a widening of the Ukraine war's reach, with a global-security lens rather than a purely European one.

stories.headline: Bangladesh vows to arrest Sheikh Hasina if she returns from India
stories.summary: Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Shama Obaed Islam, has said Dhaka will arrest former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina if she returns home, and that it expects India to honour the bilateral extradition treaty. The statement comes amid reports of Hasina's planned return in December, which has sharpened political tension in Bangladesh and triggered street violence. Dhaka's position rests on the treaty framework it shares with New Delhi, while Hasina has been residing in India since her ouster. The episode has also become entangled with the wider transition politics of Bangladesh, where the 'July Charter' reform demands and the position of BNP leader Tarique Rahman are being reshaped by the prospect of her comeback.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests India's handling of a bilateral treaty obligation against its strategic stakes in a neighbourhood in political flux — a recurring UPSC theme on India's neighbourhood policy and international law.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty and India's Extradition Act, 1962
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; bilateral treaties and international law
static.whatIsIt: A bilateral treaty between India and Bangladesh providing a legal framework for the mutual surrender of persons accused or convicted of offences, subject to conditions such as dual criminality and exceptions for political offences. In India, extradition requests are processed under the Extradition Act, 1962, which requires a treaty or arrangement with the requesting state.
static.background: The India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty was signed in January 2013, giving formal shape to cooperation on fugitives that had earlier rested on ad hoc arrangements. It has since been amended to simplify procedures and widen the scope of extraditable offences. India's domestic extradition regime is governed by the Extradition Act, 1962, which lays down the procedure for magistrates' inquiries and the role of the Central Government in accepting or rejecting requests.
static.geography: India and Bangladesh share a land border of roughly 4,096 km — the longest land border India has with any neighbour — running through West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, besides a maritime boundary settled by arbitration in 2014.
static.socioEconomic: The two countries are linked by dense trade, transit and connectivity arrangements, people-to-people ties and shared river systems; political instability in Bangladesh directly affects border trade, migration flows and India's connectivity to the North-East.
static.whyInNews: Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs said Dhaka expects India to honour the extradition treaty and that Sheikh Hasina will be arrested if she returns, amid reports of her planned December return.
static.wayForward: Any request would have to move through the treaty's legal channels and India's Extradition Act, 1962, including judicial scrutiny and the political-offence exception; India must weigh legal process against diplomatic signalling in a politically fluid neighbourhood.
prelimsPointers: India's extradition regime is governed by the Extradition Act, 1962, which requires a treaty or arrangement with the requesting country.
The India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty was signed in January 2013 and has been amended subsequently.

static.topic: India's Neighbourhood First policy and political transition in Bangladesh
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; effect of policies and politics of neighbouring countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: Neighbourhood First is India's policy of prioritising political, economic and connectivity engagement with South Asian neighbours, with Bangladesh as a principal partner under it.
static.background: India–Bangladesh ties were transformed after 1971 and deepened through instruments such as the Ganga Waters Treaty (1996), the Land Boundary Agreement (2015) and regional connectivity initiatives including BBIN. The July 2024 student-led uprising ended Sheikh Hasina's long tenure, bringing an interim arrangement and then a political transition in which the 'July Charter' reform demands and the role of BNP leader Tarique Rahman have become central. The unresolved Teesta water-sharing question and the Rohingya refugee presence remain long-standing irritants.
static.geography: Bangladesh is India's eastern neighbour, bordered by India on three sides, with a short frontier with Myanmar and a coastline on the Bay of Bengal; the Siliguri Corridor makes it strategically vital for North-East connectivity.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is among India's largest trading partners in South Asia, and the relationship covers transit, power trade, border haats, development assistance and labour migration.
static.whyInNews: Hasina's planned December return, Dhaka's arrest threat and the resulting unrest are reshaping the political calculus of Bangladesh's post-uprising transition, with direct consequences for India's engagement.
static.wayForward: India is likely to keep channels open with whichever dispensation holds power in Dhaka while insisting on treaty-based, non-political handling of the Hasina question, and to press forward on connectivity and water-sharing agendas.
prelimsPointers: The Ganga Waters Treaty was signed between India and Bangladesh in 1996.
The India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement, which exchanged enclaves, was operationalised in 2015.
BBIN (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal) is a sub-regional connectivity framework.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how political instability in Bangladesh affects the credibility of India's Neighbourhood First policy, and suggest a calibrated approach.

static.topic: Asylum, refugees and the legal status of foreign nationals in India
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — citizenship, rights of foreigners; International Relations — international law
static.whatIsIt: India has no dedicated asylum or refugee legislation. Foreigners, including those seeking protection, are governed by the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 and the Citizenship Act, 1955, with executive discretion shaping outcomes.
static.background: India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol, though it has hosted large refugee populations, including Tibetans and Sri Lankan Tamils. UNHCR operates in India and conducts refugee status determination, but its mandate is not formally embedded in domestic law. The question of sheltering a foreign political figure therefore rests on executive and diplomatic considerations rather than a statutory asylum framework.
static.whyInNews: Sheikh Hasina's continued presence in India and Dhaka's demand for her return have revived questions about the legal basis on which India hosts foreign political figures.
static.wayForward: A domestic asylum framework has been repeatedly recommended by parliamentary and expert bodies; until then, such cases will continue to be handled through executive discretion and bilateral diplomacy.
prelimsPointers: India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol.
Non-refoulement — not returning a person to a state where they face persecution — is widely regarded as a principle of customary international law.
static.mainsAngle: Should India enact a domestic asylum law? Examine in the light of its international obligations and neighbourhood sensitivities.

stories.headline: US sanctions Iran shadow banking; Tehran vows to counter 'blockade'
stories.summary: The United States has sanctioned dozens of individuals and entities accused of running Iran's 'shadow banking' networks — the opaque channels of exchange houses, front companies and intermediaries Tehran uses to move oil revenue and settle trade outside the dollar system. The designations were reported by wire agencies as targeting the enabling infrastructure rather than Iran's formal banking sector, widening the reach of US secondary-sanctions risk to third-country firms. Iran's foreign ministry responded by saying it would use 'all available means' to counter what it calls a US blockade, framing the measures as economic warfare. The exchange comes against the backdrop of an Iran–US war that, according to reports, began on 28 February 2026 when US–Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Wire, regional and Indian outlets converge on the same statements but diverge sharply on emphasis — from sanctions mechanics, to regional escalation, to the consequences for global energy flows.
stories.whyItMatters: Sanctions design, evasion networks and chokepoint risk are recurring UPSC themes under GS-II (India's West Asia policy; effect of developed-country policies on Indian interests) and GS-III (energy security, trade and the current account). Escalation in the Gulf directly affects India's crude sourcing, freight and insurance costs, diaspora remittances, and the Chabahar–INSTC connectivity route.

perspectives.take: An Indian daily framing the story through escalation and continuity of the Iran–US war, leading with Tehran's 'all available means' vow and recalling the February 2026 strikes that killed Khamenei — a view angled at implications for Indian energy and diaspora interests.

static.topic: US Secondary Sanctions and Iran's Shadow Banking Networks
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests; West Asia
static.whatIsIt: US sanctions administered chiefly by the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) that target non-US persons and entities dealing with designated Iranian banks, oil traders and exchange houses. 'Shadow banking' in this context refers to the informal network of shell companies, money-exchange houses and intermediaries — including hawala-style value-transfer channels — used to repatriate oil revenue and settle trade outside SWIFT and the dollar system.
static.background: The US has sanctioned Iran in successive waves since 1979. Iranian banks were cut off from SWIFT in 2012 and again in 2018. The 2015 JCPOA (P5+1 with Iran) lifted nuclear-related sanctions; the US withdrew in 2018 and reimposed secondary sanctions under a 'maximum pressure' approach, pushing Tehran towards informal settlement channels. Iran has long featured on the FATF's list of jurisdictions subject to a call for countermeasures. The current round targets dozens of persons and entities linked to shadow banking.
static.geography: Iran's informal settlement and oil-sales networks are commonly reported to route through the UAE, Turkey, Iraq, Malaysia and China, with the bulk of discounted crude moving eastwards to China.
static.socioEconomic: Sanctions depress the rial, stoke inflation and complicate imports of medicines and food. For India, the spillover runs through crude sourcing, freight and insurance premiums, remittances from the Gulf, and the viability of exemptions for projects such as Chabahar.
static.whyInNews: The US sanctioned dozens of individuals and entities tied to Iran's shadow banking networks in November 2026; Iran's foreign ministry said it would use 'all available means' to counter the resulting 'blockade'.
static.wayForward: India's hedges include a diversified crude basket, rupee-based or barter-style settlement where feasible, negotiated carve-outs for strategic projects, and advocacy of multilateral rather than unilateral sanctions frameworks.

static.topic: Chabahar Port and the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC)
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; bilateral and regional connectivity
static.whatIsIt: Chabahar, on Iran's Gulf of Oman coast, is India's route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan. The INSTC is a multimodal corridor linking India, Iran, Azerbaijan, Central Asia and Russia via Bandar Abbas/Chabahar and the Caspian Sea, cutting distance and freight time against the Suez route.
static.background: India, Iran and Afghanistan signed a trilateral transit agreement in 2016; India Ports Global Ltd took charge of operations at the Shahid Beheshti terminal in 2018–19 and signed a ten-year operation contract with Iran in May 2024. The US has granted limited exemptions for Chabahar-related work even under its Iran sanctions regime. The INSTC intergovernmental agreement was signed in St Petersburg in 2000 and entered into force in 2002; the Ashgabat Agreement adds a parallel multimodal route.
static.geography: Chabahar lies in Sistan-Baluchestan province, roughly 170 km west of Pakistan's Gwadar port, and is Iran's only oceanic port with direct Indian Ocean access that sits outside the Strait of Hormuz.
static.socioEconomic: The corridor promises major cuts in freight cost and transit time for India–Russia and India–Central Asia trade, supports Afghanistan's reconstruction trade, and is a focal point of India–Pakistan–China port competition in the Arabian Sea.
static.whyInNews: Fresh US sanctions rounds on Iran's financial and shipping networks raise fresh questions about the durability of exemptions covering Chabahar and INSTC traffic.
static.wayForward: Operationalise the ten-year contract, negotiate explicit carve-outs, integrate Chabahar with INSTC and the Ashgabat Agreement, and build multimodal last-mile links in Afghanistan and Central Asia.
prelimsPointers: Chabahar is Iran's only oceanic port, located on the Gulf of Oman outside the Strait of Hormuz.

static.mainsAngle: Connectivity versus sanctions: assess the viability of Chabahar and the INSTC as instruments of India's Central Asia and Eurasia strategy.

static.background: The 'tanker wars' of the 1980s, repeated Iranian threats to close the Strait during sanctions episodes, the US Fifth Fleet's presence in Bahrain, and a string of seizures and incidents since 2019 have repeatedly tested the passage.
static.geography: At its narrowest the Strait is about 33 km wide, with shipping confined to two lanes of roughly 3 km each; it is bordered by Iran to the north and Oman's Musandam peninsula to the south.

static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing across the US, Russia, Africa and Latin America, expand strategic petroleum reserves, improve refinery flexibility for heavier grades, and accelerate renewables and electrification.

static.topic: India–China Border Management and the Line of Actual Control

static.whatIsIt: The LAC is the de facto boundary between India and China, and its management rests on a layered set of bilateral agreements plus military and diplomatic mechanisms — Corps Commander-level talks, Border Personnel Meetings and the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination.
static.background: The 1993 Agreement on the Maintenance of Peace and Tranquility along the LAC and the 1996 CBM agreement form the base; the 2005 Protocol laid down modalities for CBMs. The Special Representatives mechanism dates to 2003 and the WMCC to 2012. static.socioEconomic: Border trade, transhumance and the livelihoods of border communities depend on traditional grazing and movement routes, while road, tunnel and village construction on both sides alters local demography and access.
static.whyInNews: A second round of Corps Commander-level talks was reported, focused on the Arunachal Pradesh sector, with the stated aim of setting engagement protocols and preventing face-offs between troops.

stories.headline: Chinese satellite passes over Pahalgam doubled before terror attack: reports
stories.summary: Media reports, led by an exclusive from ThePrint and followed up by The Times of India, claim that a Chinese satellite doubled its passes over Pahalgam in the days before the terror attack there, and that Chinese satellites also altered their orbits in the vicinity before and after the incident. The reports frame the timing and pattern of these orbital manoeuvres as unusual and potentially indicative of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) support extended to the perpetrators. The Times of India additionally highlights the orbit changes as raising fresh questions about a possible China link to the attack. The accounts are based on open-source orbital tracking and unnamed sources rather than any official Indian government confirmation, and no Indian agency has publicly endorsed the inference. The story feeds into a wider debate on space-based surveillance, foreign state complicity in terrorism in Jammu & Kashmir, and India's own space domain awareness.

static.background: El Niño usually weakens the monsoon; La Niña strengthens it; the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) modulates it too. The Western Ghats and Himalayan rivers (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra) define drainage; peninsular rivers are rain-fed.

stories.summary: A Hindu op-ed argues that the absence of a working nuclear risk reduction framework among the major powers is itself a growing danger, and that institutionalising restraint cannot be deferred. Its central claim is that risk reduction — hotlines, crisis communication, testing restraint and strategic dialogue — should be pursued even where formal disarmament remains stalled.

static.topic: Nuclear arms control and strategic stability architecture
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies of developed countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The body of treaties, bilateral accords and consultative mechanisms — NPT, CTBT, New START, hotlines and strategic dialogues — meant to cap arsenals, verify reductions and prevent accidental or unintended nuclear escalation.
static.background: The NPT was opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970; it recognises five nuclear weapon states (US, Russia, UK, France, China) and has near-universal membership, with India, Pakistan and Israel outside it. The CTBT, adopted in 1996, has still not entered into force. The US–Russia New START, signed in 2010 and in force from 2011, was extended in 2021 and runs to February 2026, leaving no successor bilateral strategic arms treaty in place. China, meanwhile, has expanded but never joined bilateral US–Russia formats. The result is a thinning arms control architecture at a time of sharper great-power rivalry.
static.whyInNews: An op-ed argues that a nuclear risk reduction framework cannot wait, treats Shenzhen as a possible opening, and calls for sustained engagement among Washington, Moscow and Beijing.
static.wayForward: Build layered risk reduction that does not depend on a single treaty: restore and multilateralise crisis communication channels, separate risk reduction from formal disarmament so it can advance incrementally, and use plurilateral formats to bring China into strategic stability conversations.
prelimsPointers: New START, signed in 2010 and in force from 2011, was extended in 2021 and expires in February 2026 — the last major US–Russia strategic arms treaty.

static.topic: India's nuclear doctrine and strategic autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World: foreign policy, strategic autonomy and India's nuclear position
static.whatIsIt: India's declared nuclear posture: credible minimum deterrence, no first use, civilian control through a Nuclear Command Authority, and refusal to join NPT or CTBT while seeking entry into export control regimes.
static.background: India's foreign policy draws on NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954), and was reshaped by the 1998 nuclear tests and post-1991 liberalisation. A draft nuclear doctrine was prepared by the National Security Advisory Board in 1999; the Cabinet Committee on Security issued the formal doctrine statement in 2003, which also created the Nuclear Command Authority. India joined the MTCR in 2016, the Wassenaar Arrangement in 2017 and the Australia Group in 2018, but remains outside the NSG.
static.whyInNews: Debate over nuclear risk reduction among the US, Russia and China directly bears on India's doctrine, its strategic autonomy and its stake in stable deterrence.
static.wayForward: India can combine doctrinal restraint with active advocacy for risk reduction measures — dialogue, hotlines and testing restraint — while continuing to press for NSG membership and preserving strategic autonomy across the Quad, BRICS and SCO.
prelimsPointers: India's formal nuclear doctrine statement was issued by the Cabinet Committee on Security in 2003, along with the creation of the Nuclear Command Authority.
India joined the MTCR in 2016, the Wassenaar Arrangement in 2017 and the Australia Group in 2018, but is not an NSG member.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India's doctrine of credible minimum deterrence and no first use shapes its response to a fragmenting global arms control order.

prelims: New START, the last major US–Russia strategic arms treaty, was signed in 2010, entered into force in 2011, was extended in 2021 and expires in February 2026.
The NPT entered into force in 1970 and recognises five nuclear weapon states; India, Pakistan and Israel remain outside it.
The CTBT was adopted in 1996 but has not entered into force, and India is not a signatory.
Nuclear risk reduction measures — hotlines, crisis communication and testing restraint — can advance even when formal disarmament negotiations are stalled.
stories.mainsQuestion: As the global arms control architecture erodes, nuclear risk reduction is being pursued as a substitute for disarmament. Examine the reasons for this shift and assess the implications for India's strategic autonomy.

stories.headline: Excavators near Sheshnag Lake raise ecological concerns on Amarnath route
stories.summary: Reports and photographs of JCB excavators operating close to Sheshnag Lake, a high-altitude water body on the Pahalgam route of the Amarnath Yatra in Jammu and Kashmir, have triggered concern among environmentalists and political leaders in the Valley. Critics argue that heavy machinery, muck generation and slope disturbance in a fragile, snow-fed Himalayan catchment risk sediment loading, water-quality decline and destabilisation of already landslide-prone terrain. The activity is being linked to works along the pilgrimage corridor, which sees large seasonal pilgrim movement and attendant camp, sanitation and transport infrastructure. The Tribune adds that Kashmir leaders have publicly reacted, turning an ecological question into a governance and accountability issue. No independent environmental assessment or clearance detail for the specific works has been placed in the public domain in these reports.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live test case of how environmental clearance, eco-sensitive area safeguards and disaster-risk norms apply to infrastructure in the western Himalaya, a recurring UPSC theme across GS-I geography, GS-III environment and disaster management.

perspectives.take: Frames the excavators at Sheshnag as an ecological red flag, foregrounding the absence of transparency about what the machinery is doing in a sensitive high-altitude lake catchment.
Regional (North India) framing that pairs the ecological worry with political reaction from Kashmir leaders, presenting it as both a Himalayan ecology issue and a governance/accountability question.

static.topic: High-altitude Himalayan lakes and pilgrimage-route infrastructure
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — Conservation of Himalayan ecosystems
static.whatIsIt: High-altitude lakes such as Sheshnag, on the Pahalgam route of the Amarnath Yatra, are cold, snow- and glacier-fed, nutrient-poor (oligotrophic) water bodies with slow flushing rates. Their ecology is highly sensitive to sediment inflow, construction debris, fuel spillage and any alteration of the catchment's natural drainage.
static.background: The Amarnath Yatra is an annual pilgrimage to the Amarnath cave shrine in Anantnag district, Jammu and Kashmir, approached mainly by the longer Pahalgam (south) route past Sheshnag and the shorter Baltal (north) route. Over the years the corridor has acquired tracks, camps, helipads, sanitation facilities and road improvement works. Environmentalists have repeatedly flagged debris dumping, sewage and slope cutting along the route, and cloudburst and landslide incidents have caused pilgrim casualties.
static.geography: Western (Kashmir) Himalaya, above the tree line, in the Lidder catchment; snow-fed and frozen for part of the year, with steep, unstable slopes and high seismicity.
static.socioEconomic: The yatra is a major seasonal livelihood for the Pahalgam–Baltal–Sonamarg belt — pony operators, porters, traders, transporters and hoteliers. Degradation of the lake and catchment also affects downstream water users and the wider tourism economy that depends on the landscape's health.
static.whyInNews: Excavators/JCB machines were reported working near Sheshnag Lake, prompting environmental concern and political reaction in Kashmir.
static.wayForward: Prior environmental assessment and disclosure of clearances, low-impact construction methods, carrying-capacity-based pilgrim management, scientific waste and sewage treatment, independent third-party monitoring, and restoration of disturbed slopes.
prelimsPointers: Sheshnag is a high-altitude lake on the Pahalgam route of the Amarnath Yatra; the Amarnath cave shrine lies in Anantnag district, Jammu and Kashmir.
High-altitude Himalayan lakes are typically oligotrophic and snow/glacier-fed, and recover very slowly from sediment and nutrient loading.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how pilgrimage and tourism infrastructure in the Himalaya can be reconciled with ecological integrity and disaster risk reduction.

static.topic: Environmental clearance and impact assessment for Himalayan projects
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — Environmental legislation and impact assessment
static.whatIsIt: Projects in ecologically sensitive areas require prior environmental clearance under the EIA Notification, 2006, and forest clearance under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (as amended in 2023), with additional safeguards under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and remedies under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
static.background: The EIA Notification, 2006 categorises projects as Category A (appraised centrally) and Category B (appraised at state level), and applies a 'general condition' to projects near protected areas, critically polluted areas and eco-sensitive areas. The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 governs diversion of forest land, and was substantially amended in 2023. The NGT Act, 2010 created the National Green Tribunal as a specialised body with original jurisdiction over environmental disputes. Courts have repeatedly directed that eco-sensitive zones be notified around protected areas.
static.geography: Large parts of Jammu and Kashmir, including the Kashmir Valley, fall in Seismic Zone V, the highest damage-risk category, which raises the stakes for any slope-cutting or earthwork in the region.
static.socioEconomic: Clearance regimes balance development needs against ecological costs; procedural delay raises project costs, while weak enforcement shifts environmental and health costs onto local communities and downstream users.
static.whyInNews: Earthmoving near Sheshnag Lake has revived questions about whether required assessments and clearances were obtained and disclosed for works on the pilgrimage corridor.
static.wayForward: Mandatory and publicly disclosed environmental impact assessment, cumulative-impact studies for the whole corridor rather than project-by-project appraisal, strict muck and waste management conditions, credible monitoring with penal consequences, and time-bound decision-making to avoid both delay and dilution.
prelimsPointers: EIA Notification, 2006: Category A projects are appraised by the central authority, Category B by the state-level authority.
NGT Act, 2010: the Tribunal has original jurisdiction over environmental disputes; appeals against its orders lie to the Supreme Court within 90 days.
static.mainsAngle: 'Environmental clearance in the Himalaya is often reduced to a procedural formality.' Critically examine in the light of recent infrastructure activity in ecologically sensitive mountain regions.

static.topic: Disaster risk in Himalayan pilgrimage corridors
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — Himalayan hazards and pilgrimage safety
static.whatIsIt: Pilgrimage routes in the Himalaya are exposed to landslides, cloudbursts, flash floods, avalanches and earthquakes. Unplanned construction, slope cutting and unmanaged pilgrim volumes amplify these hazards and turn natural events into disasters.
static.background: The 2013 Kedarnath floods and the 2014 Jammu and Kashmir floods are among the most cited Himalayan disaster events; cloudburst and landslide incidents have also struck the Amarnath Yatra route in recent years. The National Disaster Management Authority, constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, issues guidelines on landslides, glacial lake outburst floods and related hazards.
static.geography: Steep, deforested and road-cut slopes, narrow valleys, high seismicity (Zone V in Kashmir) and intense monsoon precipitation combine to make the corridor hazard-prone.
static.socioEconomic: Disaster risk directly threatens pilgrim safety and the seasonal livelihoods of thousands of porters, pony operators and small traders who depend on the yatra.
static.whyInNews: Heavy machinery and earthwork near Sheshnag Lake have raised fears of slope destabilisation along a route already vulnerable to landslides and cloudbursts.
static.wayForward: Hazard and risk mapping of the entire corridor, slope-stability assessment before earthwork, real-time weather and landslide early warning, regulated pilgrim numbers with staggered schedules, and trained disaster-response capacity at camps.
prelimsPointers: The National Disaster Management Authority is the apex statutory body for disaster management under the Disaster Management Act, 2005.
Kashmir and large parts of the western Himalaya lie in Seismic Zone V, the highest earthquake damage-risk zone in India.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how disaster risk reduction can be integrated into the planning and management of Himalayan pilgrimage corridors.

prelims: Sheshnag Lake lies on the Pahalgam (south) route of the Amarnath Yatra in Jammu and Kashmir; the Amarnath cave shrine is in Anantnag district.
High-altitude Himalayan lakes are typically oligotrophic, snow/glacier-fed and slow to recover from sediment or nutrient loading.
Environmental clearance for projects in ecologically sensitive areas flows from the EIA Notification, 2006, with forest clearance under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.
Kashmir and much of the western Himalaya fall in Seismic Zone V, the highest earthquake damage-risk category.
stories.mainsQuestion: The Himalayan pilgrimage economy depends on the very ecology it stresses. In the light of recent earthmoving activity near Sheshnag Lake on the Amarnath route, discuss the safeguards needed to reconcile infrastructure development with ecological integrity and disaster risk reduction in the western Himalaya.

stories.headline: Tajikistan withdraws from ICC, fourth state exit amid US pressure
stories.summary: Tajikistan has notified its withdrawal from the International Criminal Court, becoming the fourth state to do so, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger announced their exits the previous year. The three African states framed their decisions as a rejection of what they called an instrument of "neocolonial repression", while reporting on the Tajik move links the wider trend to a sustained US diplomatic push against the Court. Under the Rome Statute, a withdrawal takes effect one year after the written notification is deposited with the UN Secretary-General, and it does not automatically terminate proceedings already underway. The exits sharpen the debate over the universality of international criminal justice and the Court's exposure to geopolitical pressure.
stories.whyItMatters: Withdrawals by states parties test the universality and credibility of the Rome Statute system, a recurring theme in UPSC questions on international institutions, sovereignty versus global governance, and the politicisation of international law.

perspectives.take: Frames the story around the African precedent, foregrounding the "neocolonial repression" charge made by Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger and treating Tajikistan as the fourth in a widening set of exits.
Frames the exit as part of a trend accelerated by US diplomatic pressure on the Court, emphasising external great-power leverage rather than the states' own stated grievances.

static.topic: International Criminal Court (ICC) and the Rome Statute
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and International Institutions
static.whatIsIt: The ICC is a permanent international tribunal seated at The Hague that tries individuals — not states — for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. It was established by the Rome Statute and operates on the principle of complementarity, acting only where national jurisdictions are unwilling or unable to act.
static.background: The Rome Statute was adopted in 1998 and entered into force in 2002, creating the first permanent international criminal court, succeeding ad hoc tribunals such as those for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda. Article 127 of the Statute permits a state party to withdraw by written notification to the UN Secretary-General, with effect one year later unless a longer period is specified; withdrawal does not affect proceedings already begun. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger announced exits in the preceding year, and Tajikistan has now followed, making it the fourth such state.
static.geography: Seat of the Court: The Hague, Netherlands; the Statute is deposited with the UN Secretary-General in New York.
static.socioEconomic: African states have historically formed the largest regional bloc among states parties, and the perception that the Court has disproportionately targeted African leaders has been central to the political backlash against it.
static.whyInNews: Tajikistan became the fourth country to withdraw from the ICC, a move reported in the context of a US diplomatic push against the Court and following African withdrawals.
static.wayForward: For the Court, credibility rests on demonstrable impartiality across regions, stronger cooperation from states parties on arrests and evidence, and insulation from sanctions or diplomatic coercion by major powers.
prelimsPointers: The Rome Statute was adopted in 1998 and entered into force in 2002; the ICC sits at The Hague.
India is not a party to the Rome Statute and has not ratified it.
Withdrawal under Article 127 takes effect one year after notification to the UN Secretary-General.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether withdrawals from the Rome Statute weaken the universality of international criminal justice, and assess how the ICC can retain legitimacy amid great-power pressure.

static.topic: United Nations and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN, established in 1945, has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for Security Council expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on reform remain inconclusive.
static.geography: UN Headquarters is in New York; the International Court of Justice sits at The Hague.
static.socioEconomic: Representation deficits in multilateral bodies are increasingly linked to demands from the Global South for a greater voice in global rule-making.
static.whyInNews: The ICC withdrawals feed the broader debate on the credibility, representativeness and politicisation of multilateral institutions, of which the UN reform debate is the central example.
static.wayForward: Reform proposals centre on expanding the UNSC, restraining or qualifying the veto in mass-atrocity situations, and strengthening the voice of developing countries across multilateral bodies.
prelimsPointers: The UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The ICJ is at The Hague; UN Headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent UNSC membership rests on representativeness, population and contributions; assess the obstacles, including veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

prelims: Tajikistan is the fourth state to withdraw from the ICC, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
ICC withdrawal is governed by Article 127 of the Rome Statute and takes effect one year after notification to the UN Secretary-General.
The ICC, seated at The Hague, tries individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression, and works on the principle of complementarity.
India is not a party to the Rome Statute.
stories.mainsQuestion: Withdrawals from the Rome Statute by some states parties raise questions about the universality of international criminal justice. Examine the challenges confronting the International Criminal Court and suggest measures to strengthen its credibility and independence.

stories.headline: RBI to conduct ₹50,000-crore overnight VRR auction on November 25
stories.summary: The RBI has announced an overnight Variable Rate Repo (VRR) auction under its Liquidity Adjustment Facility for November 25, 2026. The notified amount is ₹50,000 crore for a one-day tenor, with the auction window scheduled from 09:30 AM to 10:00 AM and reversal on November 26, 2026. The central bank said the decision followed a review of current and evolving near-term liquidity conditions. Such variable-rate repo operations are used to inject liquidity into the banking system when short-term funding conditions tighten.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests understanding of RBI's liquidity management toolkit, LAF operations, and monetary policy transmission through money markets—key for GS-III economy and prelims.

static.topic: Reserve Bank of India & Monetary Policy
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: India's central bank, established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949 under the RBI Act, 1934. It conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which has a flexible inflation-targeting mandate of 4% CPI with a ±2% band. It manages liquidity using repo/reverse repo, MSF, CRR, SLR, OMOs and the Liquidity Adjustment Facility.
static.background: The MPC framework followed the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act. The RBI also regulates banks, manages forex reserves, and acts as banker to government. Its liquidity operations, including variable rate repos, help align short-term money market rates with the policy repo rate.
static.socioEconomic: Liquidity conditions influence borrowing costs for banks and ultimately credit availability to households and firms; short-term repo operations can ease temporary cash-flow mismatches in the banking system.
static.whyInNews: RBI announced an overnight Variable Rate Repo auction under LAF on November 25, 2026, for ₹50,000 crore, citing evolving near-term liquidity conditions.
static.wayForward: Continue using variable-rate liquidity tools to manage frictional and durable liquidity, while ensuring rate cuts transmit to lending rates through MCLR/EBLR and supporting fiscal-monetary coordination.
prelimsPointers: Repo = rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
MPC has 6 members: 3 RBI (Governor as chair) + 3 external; Governor has casting vote.
Inflation target: 4% CPI, band 2–6%, reviewed every 5 years.
VRR is a variable-rate liquidity injection auction under LAF; the announced operation is for ₹50,000 crore for 1 day.
static.mainsAngle: Balance growth support with price stability; examine transmission of rate cuts to borrowers and the role of liquidity management tools such as VRR in making monetary policy effective.

stories.headline: Supreme Court weighs BS-VI-only vehicle rule for Delhi-NCR
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has indicated it will consider a proposal to permit only BS-VI vehicles in Delhi-NCR, a move aimed at curbing vehicular emissions in one of the world's most polluted regions. The observation came during judicial proceedings, with the Court examining whether stricter fuel and vehicle norms can be enforced across the National Capital Region. If adopted, the restriction would affect older petrol and diesel vehicles and could reshape transport, registration and enforcement practices. The proposal is part of broader efforts to improve air quality, where the judiciary has repeatedly intervened to direct pollution-control measures.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests judicial intervention in environmental governance and the balance between public health, economic costs and federal coordination in the NCR.

perspectives.take: Reports the Court's inclination to consider a BS-VI-only regime for Delhi-NCR, framing it as a judicial push for stricter vehicular emission controls.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Art. 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Art. 214) are at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test laws and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Article 32 (SC) and 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court is considering a proposal to allow only BS-VI vehicles in Delhi-NCR, illustrating judicial review and PIL-driven environmental governance.
static.wayForward: Strengthen judicial capacity and clarify standards for judicial intervention in policy domains while ensuring executive accountability.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction: disputes between Centre and states (Art. 131).
Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.
